'''Théodore Olivier''' (1793–1853) was a French [[mathematician]].

== Life and work ==
Olivier studied in the ''Licée Imperial'' of Lyon, where he obtained in 1811 a degree in mathematics with high honours. After this, he went to the [[École Polytechnique]].<ref>{{smallcaps|Nesme}}, page 4.</ref> Olivier looked like [[Napoleon]], but nobody could prove that Olivier was an illegitimate son of the Emperor.<ref>{{smallcaps|Hervé}}, page 294.</ref>

In 1815, he was an adjunct professor in the Artillery School at [[Metz]] and, in 1819, he became a full professor. In 1821, at the request of the King of [[Sweden]], [[Charles XIV John of Sweden|Charles XIV John]] (Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte), he went to Sweden to organize the military school of Marieberg.<ref>{{smallcaps|Nesme}}, pages 5–6.</ref>

Returning to France, Oliver criticized the pedagogical system in the École Polytechnique and in 1829, jointly with [[Alphonse Lavallée]], [[Jean-Baptiste Dumas]] and [[Jean Claude Eugène Péclet]], founded the [[École Centrale de Paris|École Centrale des Arts et Manufactures]], where he was professor of geometry and mechanics for the rest of his life.<ref name="auto">{{smallcaps|Nesme}}, page 7.</ref> He also was, between 1830 and 1844, a professor at the École Polytechnique and, from 1838, a professor at the [[Arts et Métiers ParisTech|École Nationale Supérieure des Arts et Métiers]].<ref>{{smallcaps|Hervé}}, page 296.</ref>

[[File:Hiperboloide Theodore Olivier.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Example of an Olivier's geometrical model conserved in the [[Canada Science and Technology Museum]]]]
Olivier is mainly known for the construction of three-dimensional models of geometry for pedagogical purposes.<ref name="auto"/> Most of them were sold to North American institutions such as [[Union College]], [[Columbia University]] and [[United States Military Academy|West Point]], where they are preserved.<ref>{{smallcaps|Hervé}}, page 298.</ref>

Olivier also studied the theory of [[gear]]s, writing an extensive treatise on the subject and constructing models, preserved in the Musée des Arts et Offices in Paris.<ref>{{smallcaps|Hervé}}, pages 305 and follow.</ref>

Olivier had no children, but he was the uncle of the French explorer [[Aimé Olivier de Sanderval]].
